v.why: Gradient noise from tiny batches compounds through three ReLU layers into instability, so larger batches help deep nets more than shallow ones.
Strong L2 applied across more layers over-shrinks multiplicative paths and pushes deep nets toward constant outputs.
Wider nets move the function faster per Adam step, partially substituting for a tiny step size within 243 epochs.
Large fan-in multiplies per-step pre-activation changes, so raising lr reaches instability sooner in wide nets.
Large batches give fewer, less noisy updates, so they both need and tolerate bigger steps.
Very wide nets carry excess capacity that overfits small tabular sets, so explicit decay is more useful there.
sklearn scales the L2 term by 1/batch_size, so at large batches raising alpha moves toward a useful strength rather than over-regularizing.
In three-layer nets parameters grow quadratically with width, adding instability and overfitting rather than needed capacity.
Narrow layers are a capacity bottleneck that an extra layer relieves through composition.
At tiny learning rates the net is step-starved, so cutting the number of updates with larger batches hurts most.

I discarded the two hypotheses whose condition is the edited field's own value (lr up when lr is low, alpha up when alpha is high). I also dropped alpha up when lr is high, because its rationale is that collapsed training disconnects the decay effect. Among the rest, I removed near-duplicate mechanisms:

- **Depth up when batch is low:** the same noise-through-depth story as batch up when depth is high.
- **Lr up when depth is low:** the same amplification story as lr up when width is high.
- **Width up when lr is high:** this pair was already covered by width up when lr is low.
- **Alpha up when batch is low:** the same sklearn-scaling story as alpha up when batch is high.
- **Depth up when lr is mid, and batch up when lr is high:** cut to keep the field pairs distinct.
